prompt.context: It is early October, and Jimmy Smith, an MBA2 at NYU Stern, has a decision to make. After a summer interning at Firm A, Jimmy received an offer to return full-time next year. However, Jimmy also decided to re-recruit and received a competing offer from Firm B. Jimmy now needs to decide which offer he should accept, and has looked to you, his best friend, for help.
prompt.question: Which job offer should Jimmy accept?

clarifying_info.q: What does Jimmy care about most?
clarifying_info.a: Jimmy only cares about money, and is seeking to maximize financial value.
No, Jimmy is not considering any other opportunities beyond these two.

clarifying_info.q: How long does Jimmy plan to stay?
clarifying_info.a: Jimmy's intention is to work at either firm for 3 years.

clarifying_info.q: Are the two firms in the same industry?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, Firms A and B are competitors in the same industry. Firm A is considered second-tier but increasingly competes with top-tier firms for talent. Firm B is more prestigious and considered top-tier.

exhibits.title: Compensation Package by Firm
exhibits.shows: A table comparing the compensation components of Firm A and Firm B side by side.

exhibits.title: Salary Growth by Year
exhibits.shows: A chart showing projected annual salary growth over 3 years for Firm A and Firm B. Annual bonus is expected to remain constant.

data.note: Annual bonus expected to remain constant

exhibits.title: Distribution of Expected Starting Salaries for Exit Opportunities
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing the probability distribution of starting salaries at exit opportunities (after 3 years) for top-tier vs. second-tier firms, with salary levels ranging from $150k to $250k. A note states salary will grow at 5% per year indefinitely.

data.note: Assume salary will grow at 5% per year indefinitely

framework: Identify sources of value/compensation: annual salary, salary growth/raises, signing bonus, annual bonus, tuition reimbursement
Select appropriate valuation method: DCF/NPV to account for timing of cash flows
Calculate NPV for each offer over the 3-year horizon
Brainstorm additional considerations beyond immediate financials: exit opportunities, training, firm focus, firm financial performance
Evaluate exit opportunities as a key differentiator (top-tier vs. second-tier firm)

questions.prompt: Calculate the NPV of Firm A's offer over 3 years. Assume a discount rate that simplifies to roughly 10% per year (round to nearest $10k).
questions.guidance: Candidate must recognize that signing bonus is received at Year 0, tuition reimbursement at end of Year 3, and salary+bonus each year. They should discount each cash flow back to present. Strong candidates propose a DCF framework unprompted.

math.setup: Discount each year's total cash flow back to Year 0. Use simplified discounting: Year 1 / 1.1, Year 2 / 1.21 (approx 1.2), Year 3 / 1.33 (approx 1.3). The casebook simplifies further: Year 1 CF / 1.1 ≈ round down, etc.
steps: Year 3: Salary $126k + Bonus $30k + Tuition $78k = $234k; Simplified DCF ≈ $180k

questions.prompt: Calculate the NPV of Firm B's offer over 3 years using the same approach.
questions.guidance: Same DCF logic. Firm B has no tuition reimbursement, higher signing bonus, higher salary, and higher annual bonus.

math.setup: Year 0: signing bonus $40k. Years 1-3: salary + $35k annual bonus, discounted. No tuition reimbursement.
math.answer: NPV of Firm B ≈ $430k — Firm A leads by ~$10k on a 3-year basis

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, calculate the expected value of exit opportunity salaries from each firm after 3 years. Then determine whether the difference in exit opportunities changes the overall recommendation.
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute a probability-weighted expected value (mean) for each firm's exit salary distribution. They should then discount the Year 4 salary differential back to present (n=1 from the end of year 3, or effectively Year 4 = ~1.4x discount from today). The 5% growth rate mentioned in the note is a red herring — the PV of the differential already exceeds the $10k gap.

math.setup: Compute weighted average exit salary for each firm. Then PV = FV / (1+r)^n where r≈0.1 and n=4 (or simplify as FV/1.4 for Year 4).
steps: PV of $35k differential at Year 4: PV = 35 / 1.4 ≈ $25k
Alternatively using median: Firm A median ≈ $175k, Firm B median ≈ $225k; difference = $50k; PV = 50 / 1.4 ≈ $35.7k
Either way, the PV of the exit opportunity differential ($25k–$36k) exceeds the $10k NPV advantage of Firm A
CONCLUSION: Firm B becomes the better option when exit opportunities are considered
math.answer: PV of exit salary differential ≈ $25k–$36k, which exceeds Firm A's $10k NPV lead. Firm B is the better choice.

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond the financial calculations we have done, what other things should Jimmy consider before making a decision? As his friend, you should include additional financial considerations, but also introduce him to some non-financial factors he needs to think about.

categories.name: Financial
ideas: Exit opportunities and post-firm earnings potential
Firm financial stability and risk of layoffs
Negotiating leverage — use Firm A offer to extract better terms from Firm B

categories.name: Non-Financial
ideas: Focus and type of work at each firm
Brand and network value of each firm on a resume

recommendation: Jimmy should accept Firm B's offer
Although Firm A has a higher 3-year NPV (~$440k vs. ~$430k), the present value of the superior exit opportunities from top-tier Firm B ($25k–$36k PV) more than offsets this $10k gap
The long-term earnings trajectory from Firm B makes it the financially superior choice
risks: Firm B encounters financial challenges and lays off staff before Jimmy realizes the exit opportunity benefits
Jimmy underperforms at Firm B and does not achieve the higher-end exit salaries assumed in the distribution
Firm B may be a poor cultural fit and Jimmy leaves before his three years are up, forfeiting assumed benefits
next_steps: Leverage the Firm A offer to negotiate improved terms (higher signing bonus, salary) with Firm B
Conduct further due diligence on each firm including cultural fit, type of work, and team
Attend each firm's sell days and delay signing until the last possible moment to gather more information
